Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Unauthenticated mass memory deletion via mcp-memory-service DELETE /api/documents/remove-by-tags · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Unauthenticated write/read to mcp-memory-service /api/documents/* endpoints (CVE-2026-50027) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP 200 responses to the unauthenticated document-API routes (upload, batch-upload, search-content, history) on a mcp-memory-service HTTP server, where the request carried no Authorization header. This is the confidentiality/integrity half of the auth-bypass: memory poisoning via upload and stored-content disclosure via search-content/history. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable route prefixes named at documents.py source lines (upload:149, search-content:729, history) plus HTTP 200; ImWebSession's HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization lets us assert the request was truly unauthenticated, which is the article's core inconsistency (/api/memories 401 vs /api/documents 200). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator deployed the HTTP server WITHOUT MCP_API_KEY/OAuth enabled, so legitimate clients also send no Authorization header
  • Internal ingestion/backup automation that bulk-uploads documents via the same API
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing the documented CVE route
  • The operator's own PoC/pen-test traffic against 127.0.0.1
  • Health-check or uptime probes hitting /api/documents/history
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127." and SrcIpAddr != "::1"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull all SrcIpAddr hitting /api/documents/* with empty Authorization; confirm the server was launched with MCP_API_KEY/OAuth set (grep env of the memory server --http process). If auth was enabled, every unauthenticated 200 is a real bypass. 2) CONTAIN: Put the service behind the reverse proxy's auth or a WAF rule denying /api/documents/* without a valid bearer, and upgrade mcp-memory-service to >=10.67.1. 3) HUNT: For each attacker IP, correlate preceding /api/memories 401s and following DELETE /api/documents/remove-by-tags; review search-content/{upload_id} responses for exfiltrated memory content and inspect newly uploaded documents for prompt-injection payloads.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/api/documents/"
| where Url has_any ("/upload", "/batch-upload", "/search-content/", "/history")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no API key / OAuth bearer supplied = the CVE-2026-50027 bypass
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mcp-memory-service auth-bypass fingerprint: /api/memories 401 then /api/documents 200 from same source AIExploitation High
Correlates the CVE-2026-50027 PoC signature on a single source IP: a 401 on the correctly-protected /api/memories endpoint followed within the hour by a successful (200) request to a /api/documents/* route with no credentials. This two-event shape is far higher fidelity than either request alone because it captures an attacker discovering the inconsistent auth boundary and pivoting to the unprotected router. Rationale: Directly models the PoC attack chain (STEP 1 GET /api/memories -> 401, STEP 4/5 POST/DELETE /api/documents/* -> 200) as a same-source temporal correlation; the 401-then-200 pairing is the article's own proof that the attacker found and exploited the inconsistent auth boundary, making it very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured legitimate client whose token expired (401 on /api/memories) while a separate unauthenticated automation happens to hit /api/documents from the same NAT egress IP
  • Security scanner walking every route and recording both a 401 and a 200 from one host
  • Shared corporate proxy/NAT collapsing many users behind one SrcIpAddr
  • Operator testing both endpoints during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source IP is not a known internal proxy/scanner; inspect the exact /api/documents route that returned 200 (upload = poisoning, search-content = read, remove* = destruction). 2) CONTAIN: Block the source at the WAF/reverse proxy, disable the /api/documents/* router or gate it behind auth, and upgrade to mcp-memory-service >=10.67.1. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every upload_id this IP created or deleted; snapshot current memory store contents, diff against last known-good backup, and purge attacker-injected documents to prevent downstream prompt-injection of the AI agent.
let window = 1h;
let probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where Url has "/api/memories" and HttpStatusCode == 401
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/api/documents/" and HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| join kind=inner probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + window)
| project ProbeTime, BypassTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url
| order by BypassTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/memories*" OR Web.url="*/api/documents/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval memories_401=if(like(url,"%/api/memories%") AND status=401, count, 0)
| eval docs_bypass=if(like(url,"%/api/documents/%") AND status=200, count, 0)
| stats sum(memories_401) as memories_401, sum(docs_bypass) as docs_bypass, values(url) as urls, values(dest) as dest, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by src
| where memories_401 > 0 AND docs_bypass > 0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/memories*" OR Web.url="*/api/documents/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval memories_401=if(like(url,"%/api/memories%") AND status=401, count, 0)
| eval docs_bypass=if(like(url,"%/api/documents/%") AND status=200, count, 0)
| stats sum(memories_401) as memories_401, sum(docs_bypass) as docs_bypass, values(url) as urls, values(dest) as dest, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by src
| where memories_401 > 0 AND docs_bypass > 0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Unauthenticated mass memory deletion via mcp-memory-service DELETE /api/documents/remove-by-tags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful (200) DELETE requests to the unauthenticated /api/documents/remove-by-tags and /api/documents/remove/{upload_id} routes — the availability/integrity impact of CVE-2026-50027 where an attacker permanently destroys memories belonging to authenticated users without credentials. A burst of such DELETEs from one source is a destruction event. Rationale: Uses the specific destructive routes and sink named in the article (remove-by-tags -> storage.delete_by_tags at line 705, remove/{upload_id}) constrained to DELETE + 200; a successful unauthenticated DELETE to these paths is by definition the CVE's availability impact (STEP 5 memories_deleted=1) with essentially no benign equivalent when auth is enabled. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1485 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin housekeeping that prunes documents by tag through the same API
  • Automated retention/cleanup job deleting expired memories
  • Operator running the published PoC (tag cve-poc) during validation
  • Server started without MCP_API_KEY so all DELETEs are legitimately unauthenticated
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127." and SrcIpAddr != "::1"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the DELETEs are unauthenticated (empty Authorization) and the server was configured with auth; count how many upload_ids/tags were removed and from which SrcIpAddr. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately block the source, take the HTTP server offline or gate /api/documents/* behind auth, upgrade to >=10.67.1, and freeze the storage backend for forensic capture before it is overwritten. 3) HUNT: Restore deleted memories from the most recent backup, diff to quantify loss, and pivot on the same IP for prior upload (poisoning) and search-content (exfiltration) calls to scope the full read/write/delete blast radius.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE"
| where Url has_any ("/api/documents/remove-by-tags", "/api/documents/remove/")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| summarize DeleteCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Urls = make_set(Url, 20) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by DeleteCount desc

BeepRAT (DCRat variant) delivered as HFY.exe telephone-management .NET app from archive AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of HFY.exe, the .NET 'phone number management' decoy that Rubrik Zero Labs attributes to the China-nexus BeepRAT multi-stage loader, especially when launched from an archive-extraction path (Downloads/Temp) alongside database-driver DLLs. Article-specific because HFY.exe is the named first-stage binary of this campaign. Rationale: HFY.exe is the specifically-named .NET decoy binary from Rubrik Zero Labs; pairing it with archive-extraction parent processes/paths distinguishes the BeepRAT infection from any unrelated file of the same short name. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate in-house or third-party utility genuinely named HFY.exe run by a user
  • IT deploying a benign telephony/PBX management tool from a Downloads folder
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox host onboarded to the tenant
  • Software-packaging team staging installers under \Temp\ that include an unrelated HFY.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ProgramData\\Package Cache","\\Program Files\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and check it against Rubrik's BeepRAT sample and VT/ThreatFox; inspect sibling files in the same folder for database-driver DLLs bundled with the ZIP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the HFY.exe process tree, and quarantine the extraction directory. 3) Hunt: on the same device look for a new scheduled task (UC2), DoH lookups / api.service.bio beacons (UC3), and in-memory .NET assembly loads; sweep the org for the same SHA256 and archive filename.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HFY.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Desktop\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","winrar.exe","7zg.exe","7zfm.exe","7z.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\HFY.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BeepRAT HFY.exe Telephone-Management Decoy Execution

BeepRAT scheduled-task persistence created by HFY.exe loader AIInstallation Medium
Hunts schtasks.exe /create (or a scheduled-task registration) whose parent is the BeepRAT decoy HFY.exe or a binary running from an archive-extraction path — the persistence mechanism Rubrik documented for this China-nexus RAT. Article-specific via the HFY.exe parent pivot rather than a generic schtasks alert. Rationale: The article states BeepRAT 'establishes persistence on the host via scheduled tasks'; anchoring the schtasks /create on the HFY.exe parent (or archive-path executable parent) keeps this specific to the campaign instead of a generic scheduled-task rule. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign app legitimately named HFY.exe that registers an updater scheduled task
  • Portable software run from Downloads that self-registers a maintenance task
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample generating expected persistence
  • An installer temporarily extracted to \Temp\ that creates a first-run task
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks command line to capture the task name, trigger, and the executable it points to; verify the pointed-to binary hash. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate the host, and kill HFY.exe. 3) Hunt: confirm the HFY.exe drop (UC1) and outbound DoH/api.service.bio beacon (UC3); search other hosts for a scheduled task pointing at the same payload path or referencing the same task name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe"
   or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\") and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create"
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\HFY.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BeepRAT Scheduled Task Persistence via HFY.exe

description: Detects schtasks.exe /create spawned by the BeepRAT decoy HFY.exe, the persistence step reported by Rubrik Zero Labs.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/HFY\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.parent_process_name="HFY.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
BeepRAT DoH-based C2 resolution and api.service.bio beacon AICommand & Control High
Hunts the BeepRAT command-and-control channel: direct contact with the C2 domain api.service.bio, or the HFY.exe loader issuing DNS-over-HTTPS lookups to public DoH resolvers to covertly resolve its C2 (as Rubrik documented). Article-specific via the exact C2 domain plus the non-browser DoH pivot. Rationale: api.service.bio is the article/Rubrik-linked C2 domain (highest-fidelity IOC); the DoH-resolver clause catches the documented DNS-over-HTTPS resolution when the domain itself is hidden from plaintext DNS. Note: because BeepRAT uses DoH, plaintext DNS logs may not show api.service.bio — the DeviceNetworkEvents/DoH-provider path covers that gap. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app coincidentally resolving api.service.bio if the domain is ever repurposed
  • A non-browser enterprise app configured to use DoH resolvers for privacy
  • Security tooling / EDR that itself performs DoH lookups
  • A user-installed DoH proxy (e.g. a privacy client) generating resolver traffic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedgewebview2.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and confirm whether it is HFY.exe or an unsigned/.NET binary; capture the resolved IP behind api.service.bio. 2) Contain: block api.service.bio and the resolved C2 IP at egress, isolate the host, and kill the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IP across all hosts, correlate with HFY.exe execution (UC1) and scheduled-task persistence (UC2), and review for data staging preceding exfil since BeepRAT lacks egress restrictions.
let DoHResolvers = dynamic(["cloudflare-dns.com","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","chrome.cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","doh.opendns.com","dns.quad9.net","doh.cleanbrowsing.org"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "api.service.bio"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe" and RemoteUrl in~ (DoHResolvers))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname =~ "api.service.bio" or Url has "api.service.bio"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INTERPOL law-enforcement lure delivering ransomware via Proton Drive archive AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails impersonating INTERPOL / law-enforcement 'investigation' notices that direct recipients to a Proton Drive URL hosting a password-protected archive, the delivery chain Bitdefender tied to a custom ransomware payload targeting SMBs. Article-specific via the law-enforcement lure + Proton Drive hosting combination. Rationale: Combines Bitdefender's specifics — impersonation of law enforcement (INTERPOL) as the lure and Proton Drive (drive.proton.me) as the delivery host for a password-protected archive — a pairing distinctive to this campaign. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon left empty because the detection is bound to Defender EmailEvents+EmailUrlInfo mailflow telemetry with no clean equivalent on those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business partner genuinely sharing a file via Proton Drive to an inbox
  • Internal compliance/legal team circulating a real investigation notice with an 'evidence' subject
  • Privacy-conscious users who routinely receive Proton Drive share links
  • Newsletter or press email discussing an INTERPOL operation matching the subject keywords
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the sender domain/SPF-DKIM-DMARC on AuthenticationDetails and open the Proton Drive URL in a sandbox to capture the hosted archive and password. 2) Contain: purge the message from all recipient mailboxes (soft-delete/ZAP), block the sender and the specific Proton Drive share URL, and warn recipients not to open it. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents for anyone who clicked, then correlate to endpoint archive extraction and subsequent mass file-encryption / ransom-note activity on those users' devices.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where UrlDomain has "proton"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("drive.proton.me","proton.me") or Url has "drive.proton.me"
| where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","law enforcement","police","evidence","suspicious activity","criminal")
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject,
          Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where UrlDomain has "proton"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("drive.proton.me","proton.me") or Url has "drive.proton.me"
| where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","law enforcement","police","evidence","suspicious activity","criminal")
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject,
          Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Platform-aware phishing: Ninite Loader delivering ConnectWise/Itarian RAT on Windows AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Cofense-reported chain where a fingerprinted Windows victim receives Ninite Loader, which then installs the trusted-but-abused ConnectWise ScreenConnect client (or Itarian RAT) as a remote-access trojan — flagged when the RMM/loader is spawned by a browser or from a download path. Article-specific via the Ninite Loader → ConnectWise/Itarian pivot. Rationale: Uses Cofense's named tools — Ninite Loader as the delivery loader and ConnectWise ScreenConnect / Itarian RAT as the repurposed remote-access payloads — constrained to a browser/loader parent so it catches phishing-driven RMM installs rather than sanctioned deployments. Kept hunting-tier because ConnectWise is dual-use. Cross-checked against: • https://cofense.com/blog/the-platform-you-trust-is-the-platform-they-target • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/phishing-campaigns-auto-adapt-victims-device-os • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying ConnectWise ScreenConnect for remote support
  • A user intentionally downloading the real Ninite installer from ninite.com to install apps
  • An MSP-managed endpoint where ScreenConnect is the sanctioned RMM
  • A pentest/red-team engagement using ScreenConnect as an approved C2/RMM
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("relay.screenconnect.com/e=Support") and DeviceName in~ ("HELPDESK-RMM-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether ScreenConnect/Itarian is a sanctioned RMM for this host; inspect the ScreenConnect relay/instance ID in the command line and compare to your approved tenant. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, uninstall/kill the ScreenConnect client and Ninite Loader, and block the attacker relay domain. 3) Hunt: review the preceding browser download URL for the fingerprinting landing page, check macOS/Android users hitting the same URL for credential-harvest redirects, and sweep for the same relay instance ID across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ConnectWise"
         or FileName has "ScreenConnect"
         or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","connectwisecontrol.com","relay.screenconnect.com","Itarian","itarian.com")
         or FileName has_any ("Ninite","Itarian"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","Ninite","Itarian") or CommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","connectwisecontrol.com","relay.screenconnect.com","itarian.com")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as ToddyCat has been attributed to a new malware called Umbrij that's designed to gain surreptitious access to a victim's email correspondence via the Google API. "In this campaign, the attackers focused their attention on corporate email communications hosted on Gmail, targeting access compromise via APIs," Kaspersky said in a detailed report published this week. "

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1528

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading via signed BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop · [LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Headless Chromium remote-debugging launched against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) · [LLM] Google OAuth endpoint reached by browser spawned from Umbrij side-load binary
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser credential store copied into %LOCALAPPDATA% BackupFiles staging directory · [LLM] OAuth grant / API access to 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' app (Umbrij token abuse) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading via signed BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific DLL side-loading chain ToddyCat uses to launch the Umbrij .NET stealer: three legitimate signed binaries each insecurely loading a named rogue DLL. Article-specific because it pairs each abused host binary with its exact malicious module name and hash rather than generic side-loading. Rationale: Uses the exact abused host binaries (BDSubWiz.exe/VSTestVideoRecorder.exe/GoogleDesktop.exe), their paired rogue DLL names, the Umbrij DLL MD5s (28cb7b26.../bae82a15.../9f5f2f0f...), and the anomalous drop paths confirmed by Securelist. The binary+DLL pairing is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/ • https://cyberpress.org/toddycat-automates-gmail-compromise/
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by anomalous-path filter)
  • Genuine Visual Studio test agent running VSTestVideoRecorder.exe from the VS install tree
  • A developer manually placing a signed tool in C:\Users\Public for testing
  • Security tooling copying signed binaries to Temp during sandbox detonation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files\Bitdefender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading binary runs from Temp/Vss/Public and the loaded DLL name/hash matches (log.dll, GoogleServices.dll, or the VideoRecorderEngine DLL). Pull the DLL and check signer/ConfuserEx obfuscation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the side-loading process, quarantine the rogue DLL and the co-located signed EXE. 3) Hunt: search the same host and user for the scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp', a %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\BackupFiles directory, and headless-browser remote-debugging launches (UC3/UC4).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "BDSubWiz.exe" and FileName =~ "log.dll")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
    or MD5 in~ ("28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1","bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66","9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel has no native image-load table; pivot on the host binary executing from an anomalous location (Umbrij drop paths)
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\Vss\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/execution primitive Umbrij used: a scheduled task named after Kaspersky's EDR agent that launches the digitally signed side-loading binary. Article-specific because it keys on the exact impersonated task name Kaspersky reported during its threat hunt. Rationale: Keys on the exact impersonated task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' reported by Kaspersky; a scheduled task with that name not created by a genuine Kaspersky process is an unambiguous ToddyCat indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kaspersky Endpoint Security installer/updater registering its own EDR task (excluded by initiating-process filter)
  • Backup/imaging tools cloning a host that legitimately runs Kaspersky and replaying task XML
  • Sysadmin manually re-creating a Kaspersky task after repair
  • SCCM/Intune redeploying Kaspersky agent
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Kaspersky Lab\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action/XML — confirm it launches a signed binary (BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop) from Temp/Vss/Public rather than the real Kaspersky path, and identify the creating process. 2) Contain: delete the rogue task, isolate the host, quarantine the referenced binary+DLL. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (side-load), and check for BackupFiles browser-profile copies and headless remote-debugging launches on the same host/user.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
| where AdditionalFields has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" or ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("avp.exe","kavfsslp.exe")   // exclude genuine Kaspersky-created tasks
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698   // scheduled task created
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Headless Chromium remote-debugging launched against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the core Shadow Token via Remote Debug (STRD) step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge headless with a remote debugging port pointed at a copied user profile in BackupFiles to hijack the live Gmail session. Article-specific via the exact flag+path combination. Rationale: Combines the exact Chromium flag (--remote-debugging-port) with the article's attacker-specific staging folder 'BackupFiles'; no legitimate workflow launches a browser headless-debugging against a copied BackupFiles profile. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/
ATT&CKT1185 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright automated UI test suites launching headless Chrome with remote-debugging (won't reference BackupFiles)
  • Selenium/browser-automation CI runners on developer endpoints
  • Manual developer debugging with --remote-debugging-port against a normal profile path
  • Enterprise screenshot/monitoring tools driving Chrome headless
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm --user-data-dir points into a BackupFiles folder and identify the parent process (expect a side-load binary). Grep the host for the Umbrij log file containing an OAuth authorization code. 2) Contain: kill the browser+parent, isolate host, and initiate Google Workspace token revocation for the affected user. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC5 (OAuth network flow) and UC6 (Google Workspace Migration/Sync app grant) for the same user, and revoke sessions in Google Admin.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser credential store copied into %LOCALAPPDATA% BackupFiles staging directory AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Umbrij's profile-theft step: copying Login Data, Web Data, cookies and Local/IndexedDB storage of each authenticated profile into a BackupFiles directory under the Chrome/Edge app-data path. Article-specific via the exact folder and the named profile artifacts. Rationale: Keys on the exact attacker-created 'BackupFiles' subfolder under the Chrome/Edge LocalAppData path plus the named profile artifacts (Login Data, Web Data, cookies, IndexedDB); browsers never write those files into a BackupFiles directory, and the non-browser initiating process makes it high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/migration utility that literally names its folder 'BackupFiles' and copies browser profiles (rare; verify initiating process)
  • Browser profile-migration tools during OS upgrade
  • IT-driven roaming-profile sync copying Login Data
  • User manually backing up a browser profile into a folder coincidentally named BackupFiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","browsermigration.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process that wrote into BackupFiles (expect a side-load binary, not chrome/msedge) and enumerate which profiles/emails were staged. 2) Contain: isolate host, remove the BackupFiles directory after forensic capture, and force-reset the affected user's browser sessions and Google Workspace tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC3 headless remote-debug launch and UC6 Google Workspace app grant on the same user; assume cookie/session theft and rotate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "BackupFiles"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","Web Data","Preferences","Secure Preferences","Cookies") or FolderPath has_any ("IndexedDB","Local Storage","Network")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "BackupFiles"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Login Data","Web Data","Preferences","Secure Preferences","IndexedDB","Local Storage","Network","Cookies")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\BackupFiles\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Edge\\BackupFiles\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Google OAuth endpoint reached by browser spawned from Umbrij side-load binary AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the STRD token-acquisition network step: a Chrome/Edge process spawned by one of the abused side-load host binaries contacts accounts.google.com / oauth2.googleapis.com to drive the OAuth consent-and-token flow. Article-specific via the parent-process chain, not generic Google traffic. Rationale: The fidelity comes from the parent chain — a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop hitting Google OAuth endpoints — plus the specific client project IDs 279448736670/1095133494869 (Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Outlook) in the proxy URL where available; plain accounts.google.com traffic alone is filtered out by the parent predicate. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://cyberpress.org/toddycat-automates-gmail-compromise/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal user browsing to accounts.google.com (excluded — requires side-load parent or remote-debugging flag)
  • Legit Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Outlook actually deployed and used by the org (validate at myaccount.google.com/connections)
  • Browser automation frameworks authenticating to Google
  • Enterprise SSO flows to oauth2.googleapis.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser's parent is a side-load host binary (or the remote-debugging flag is present) and capture the full OAuth URL/client_id from proxy logs. 2) Contain: isolate host, and in Google Admin revoke the 'Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook' authorization and force token/session invalidation for the user. 3) Hunt: search UC6 for subsequent Gmail/Drive/Contacts API access via that app, and check the Umbrij log file for the exfiltrated authorization code.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("accounts.google.com","oauth2.googleapis.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires web-proxy telemetry that captures the full OAuth request URL/query
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "accounts.google.com/o/oauth2" or Url has "oauth2.googleapis.com"
| where Url has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")   // Google Workspace Migration / Sync for Outlook client project IDs
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MSEdge.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:accounts.google.com OR @DestinationHostname:oauth2.googleapis.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(accounts\.google\.com|oauth2\.googleapis\.com)$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ParentBaseFileName=/\\?(BDSubWiz|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i}, field=[ContextProcessId], key=[TargetProcessId], include=[ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
OAuth grant / API access to 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' app (Umbrij token abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the objective of the STRD attack: an OAuth authorization and subsequent Gmail/Drive/Contacts API access via the Google Workspace Migration or Sync for Microsoft Outlook application, whose client IDs Umbrij drives to mint tokens. Article-specific via the exact abused app names and client project IDs. Rationale: Uses the exact application names ('Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook') Kaspersky told defenders to look for at myaccount.google.com/connections, plus the corroborated client project IDs 279448736670/1095133494869; token grants to these apps in an org that doesn't use them are a direct Umbrij indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Org genuinely migrating mailboxes from Exchange/Outlook into Google Workspace (validate with IT — legitimate Migration tool use)
  • Users who legitimately run Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook
  • Admin-approved third-party marketplace OAuth apps with similar scopes
  • A one-off sanctioned data-import project
Response runbook
1) Triage: at myaccount.google.com/connections (or Google Admin > Security > API controls) confirm whether the Migration/Sync app is sanctioned; review IP/geo/user-agent and the granted Gmail/Drive/Contacts/Calendar scopes. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke the app's access to invalidate all issued OAuth tokens and force-reauth the user. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users who granted the same app, review Gmail API read volume (users.messages.list/get) for bulk export, and correlate to the endpoint chain (UC1–UC5).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or AdditionalFields has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ObjectName, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or AdditionalFields has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ObjectName, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

DeviceFileEvents

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"

OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
